expert_decisions.note: A is the concert tonic; the riff is A-blues/modal, so its flat-third and flat-seventh content can make profile matching report Am even though a plain A label is the better original-recording key.
The recording is D-centered minor/blues-modal: the verse riff and vocal use the minor collection, and the detailed opening-window profiles strongly select Dm. The full-preview D label loses the mode.

The matched audio is the TELYKast remix, but the standard Imagine Dragons original is clearly established in Eb major. The remix's Cm result is the relative-minor reading, not evidence for the original key.
Everlong resolves to D and is conventionally D major/modal; Bm is its relative minor. Temperley also selected D, while the other profiles over-weighted the shared pitch collection.

Deezer matched Weezer's different song I Don't Want To Let You Go. The body supplies no recording evidence, and the D performance chart alone is insufficient to assert the original-recording key conservatively.
The original is centered in D minor; F is its relative major and is prominent in the sampled section. The Dm-F-Bb-C harmonic material explains the profile confusion.
The song is a C-centered major/blues vamp rather than functional C minor. Blues flat thirds and sevenths explain the Cm profile; the canonical performance chart also keeps the tonic at C.

The original arrangement has a G tonal center with substantial modal/chromatic mixture. The preview covers C-heavy material, but C is not the song's global tonic; the canonical G chart is consistent with the recording.
The global loop and melodic resolution center B minor. A and E dominate parts of the excerpt, but the detailed first window selects Bm and the full A result is a section/tonic error.

The original is G-centered with unusually chromatic major/minor mixture. A higher-resolution aggregate of the cached preview selects G across the tested profiles; Abm is a section-driven semitone/mode failure.
The canonical lyrics identify Crash Into Me; 'Crash' is only the local shorthand title, so the Deezer match is semantically correct. The recording and the performance chart both support E.
The Sublime recording centers G minor/G Dorian. Its characteristic Gm-C vamp makes C major attractive to profile matching, but G remains the tonic; the canonical performance key agrees.
The recording is E-centered minor/blues-modal. Power chords and the major-inflected E sonority cause some profiles to omit the minor mode, but the riff and later window establish Em.
The original centers E minor; G is the relative major and dominates the sampled opening. Later-window profiles move to Em, and the canonical Em performance chart matches the song's tonic.

E major is a defensible global key for the original: every profile in each detailed preview window selects E, with repeated long E sonorities. C#m is the relative-minor/verse-centered performance reading, not a clear basis to overturn E.
The low-tuned main riff and harmonic center are C minor/modal. Major-oriented profiles flatten the mode to C, while the detailed chord evidence and minor-sensitive profiles consistently favor Cm.
The progression and melodic resolution center F# minor. A is the relative major; the minor-sensitive detailed profiles shift to F#m, especially in the later window.
The Otis Redding recording is plainly G major. Em is the relative-minor profile reading and does not match the verse, chorus, or final G-centered resolution.
The repeating Bm-A-E progression resolves to B minor, with a Dorian major-IV color. The E-heavy preview is a tonic-selection error, not E major; the canonical Bm chart agrees.
Deezer supplied the River Plate live version, but the original studio recording's E-centered major/blues key is unequivocal. The live preview's Ab result is unrelated to the song's tonic.

The matched track is a live version and its excerpt emphasizes D/A material. The original studio song is clearly E-minor-centered, later contrasting with an E-centered rock section; the canonical E chart reflects the tonic, not concert major mode.

The recording's concert bass and chord content center E minor, with G as the relative-major collection. The cached preview repeatedly exposes E/D/G roots; a D label should not be inferred merely from alternate down-tuned guitar notation.

Ab is the concert-pitch blues tonic of the SRV recording. The guitar is commonly treated as an A-shape performance with the instrument tuned down a semitone; that fingering must not be mislabeled as concert A or Eb.
The verse bass line and vocal cadence center A minor. C is the relative major and dominates portions of the preview, while the later detailed window correctly selects Am.
The cached original recording consistently centers C#/Db, with F# as the main contrasting area. The D performance key is a playable/fingering transposition; it should not override the concert pitch.

The studio arrangement resolves to D and is best labeled D major/modal. Its prominent Am and C material can mislead a short-window profile, but later windows and the canonical D chart recover the global tonic.
